what.text: Papaverine is an alkaloid obtained from opium or made synthetically. The label says it lacks the chemical ring (phenanthrene group) found in morphine and codeine, and has minimal effects on the brain. In the US it is sold as a prescription injection for spasm of smooth muscle, but this injection has never been FDA approved.

what.text: How it acts, according to the label

items.text: Papaverine relaxes smooth muscle directly, especially in large arteries and when the muscle is in spasm. This includes blood vessels and the gut, bile and urinary tracts.

src.label: Papaverine HCl injection label (American Regent), Clinical pharmacology

items.text: It is broken down in the liver, and about 90% is bound to blood proteins.

src.label: Papaverine HCl injection label (American Regent), Clinical pharmacology

what.text: For erectile dysfunction (ED), papaverine has been injected into the penis (intracavernosal injection), alone, mixed with phentolamine, or mixed with phentolamine and alprostadil ("Trimix"). These mixes are compounded and are not FDA approved. Two-drug mixes are called "Bimix" in some papers, but the name does not mean one recipe: one 2025 paper used it for papaverine with chlorpromazine.

research.text: A 1982 letter in The Lancet reported injecting papaverine into the penis for ED. The published human studies found are small comparisons from the 1990s and 2000s. No large placebo-controlled trial of papaverine for ED, alone or in a mix, was found.
That report was a one-page letter in The Lancet in 1982 by R. Virag on injecting papaverine into the penis for erectile failure. PubMed has no abstract, and the full letter was not read here.

research.title: Papaverine plus phentolamine vs alprostadil (J Urol 1997)

facts.v: Bechara A, Casabé A, Chéliz G, et al. J Urol 1997;157(6):2132-4
randomized into 6 groups, each tested with both solutions and placebo, 1 week apart
60 men (mean age 58) with ED for more than 6 months, during erection testing
1 mL of papaverine 30 mg/mL plus phentolamine 0.5 mg/mL, or 1 mL of alprostadil 30 micrograms/mL, injected into the penis
single test injections
erection good enough for penetration; short-term side effects

research.found: 54% responded to papaverine plus phentolamine and 50% to alprostadil (not significantly different). Prolonged erection occurred in 18% and 15%. Pain was reported by 15% with papaverine plus phentolamine and 35% with alprostadil (P < 0.05).

src.label: Bechara et al., J Urol, PubMed

research.title: Trimix doses vs alprostadil alone (Int J Impot Res 2005)

facts.v: Seyam R, Mohamed K, Akhras AA, Rashwan H. Int J Impot Res 2005;17(4):346-53
prospective; 9 groups of Trimix doses; each man got alprostadil 20 micrograms and one Trimix dose, 1 week apart
180 men with ED; mean age 50.5
Trimix (phentolamine 1 mg, alprostadil 2.5 to 10 micrograms, papaverine 5 to 20 mg) vs alprostadil alone
two clinic visits
penile artery flow on ultrasound, rigidity, satisfaction, side effects

research.found: Blood flow, rigidity, pain and satisfaction did not differ significantly. Trimix gave longer erections and more priapism than alprostadil alone.

src.label: Seyam et al., Int J Impot Res, PubMed

research.title: Liver tests during papaverine self-injection (Urology 1998)

facts.v: Brown SL, Haas CA, Koehler M, et al. Urology 1998;52(5):844-7
review of records, October 1994 to June 1996, with an age-matched comparison group
30 men injecting papaverine or papaverine/phentolamine; 20 men without ED
mean follow-up 18 months
liver function tests

research.found: 2 of 30 men (6.7%) had raised liver tests during treatment; both had a history of alcohol abuse and neither had symptoms. 1 of 20 men in the comparison group had a raised bilirubin.

src.label: Brown et al., Urology, PubMed

research.title: Errors in an injection program (J Sex Med 2024)

facts.v: Furtado TP, Teloken PE, Ortega Y, et al. J Sex Med 2024;21(6):529-32
review of records of men using injections for 6 months or more at one cancer center
1,368 men; agents used were Trimix (62%), Bimix (35%), papaverine alone (2%) and alprostadil alone (1%)
mean follow-up 3.2 years
self-injection errors

research.found: 42% of men made at least one error. Errors that can lead to priapism included changing their own dose (5%) and injecting twice (4%). Younger age, graduate education and under 12 months of use predicted major errors.

src.label: Furtado et al., J Sex Med, PubMed

us.text: No papaverine product is FDA approved. Papaverine injection is sold by prescription as an unapproved drug, and its label says it is not for injection into the penis for impotence. Compounded Bimix and Trimix are not FDA approved. As of November 1, 2026.

items.text: FDA's Drugs@FDA data list no approved papaverine product. DailyMed lists papaverine injection labels with the marketing category "unapproved drug other".

items.text: the label states: "Papaverine Hydrochloride is not indicated for the treatment of impotence by intracorporeal injection. The intracorporeal injection of papaverine hydrochloride has been reported to have resulted in persistent priapism requiring medical and surgical intervention." Injecting it into the penis is off-label.

world.lead: Papaverine injection is an authorised prescription medicine in Australia and Canada. In the US it is sold without FDA approval. No EU-wide authorisation exists. No regulator record found here lists ED as an approved use. It is not on WADA's Prohibited List.

after.text: Papaverine is not named on the WADA 2026 Prohibited List or on the 2027 List, which takes effect January 1, 2027. It is not in the 2027 Monitoring Program either. Class S0 covers only substances with no current government approval for human therapeutic use, and papaverine is approved for some use (see above).

side.text: Injected into the penis, papaverine can cause priapism, an erection that will not go down, which can need emergency treatment. The injection label also lists liver inflammation (hepatitis), heart rhythm problems and dependence.

items.text: the label says injection into the penis has been reported to cause persistent priapism needing medical and surgical treatment. In the 1997 trial, 18% of men had a prolonged erection after papaverine plus phentolamine. In the 2005 trial, Trimix caused more priapism than alprostadil alone.

items.text: injection into a vein must not be used with complete heart block; where conduction is slowed it may cause extra or fast beats from the ventricles.

items.text: hepatitis, probably immune-related, has been reported infrequently and has rarely progressed to cirrhosis. The label says to stop if jaundice, eosinophilia or abnormal liver tests appear. One review of 30 men injecting papaverine found raised liver tests in 2.

items.text: nausea, stomach discomfort, loss of appetite, constipation or diarrhea, rash, malaise, vertigo, headache, intense facial flushing, sweating, faster heart rate, a slight rise in blood pressure and excessive sleepiness. Caution with glaucoma.
